scenario: WIBTA for going on a trip my wife can no longer go on because of her DUI? | Last year, my wife and I made plans to spend a week in Montreal with another couple we're close friends with. None of us had been to Canada before, and we thought it would be fun if we all went together. We requested time off work, bought flights, made hotel reservations, etc. The trip is scheduled for March. Here's the problem: a month we made all these arrangements, my wife was arrested for drunk driving, and she pleaded guilty to the charge this week. My understanding is that she can no longer enter Canada with a DUI on her record. But I still want to go on the trip, which I paid a lot of money for, and I told our friends I still plan on accompanying them. My wife and I got into a huge fight over it, and she accused me of being selfish and unsupportive for wanting to go without her. I don't think that's fair. I've supported her throughout the entire court process, which has been incredibly stressful and expensive, and I've been looking forward to this trip for a long time. WIBTA?

None of us had been to Canada before, and we thought it would be fun if we all went together. We requested time off work, bought flights, made hotel reservations, etc. The trip is scheduled for March. Here's the problem: a month we made all these arrangements, my wife was arrested for drunk driving, and she pleaded guilty to the charge this week. My understanding is that she can no longer enter Canada with a DUI on her record. But I still want to go on the trip, which I paid a lot of money for, and I told our friends I still plan on accompanying them. My wife and I got into a huge fight over it, and she accused me of being selfish and unsupportive for wanting to go without her. I don't think that's fair. I've supported her throughout the entire court process, which has been incredibly stressful and expensive, and I've been looking forward to this trip for a long time. WIBTA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: I'll provide a neutral, analytical response. In this scenario, I would say: 1 (You Are The Asshole). Here's why: while it's understandable that you've been looking forward to the trip and have invested time and money into it, your wife's situation has changed significantly due to her DUI. She's not only facing the consequences of her actions but also feeling embarrassed, ashamed, and possibly anxious about not being able to join the trip. By choosing to go on the trip without her, you're essentially leaving her behind during a difficult time. This might be perceived as insensitive and unsupportive, especially given the emotional turmoil she's already experiencing. It's not just about the trip; it's about being there for your partner when they need you. It's also worth considering that your wife might be feeling guilty, regretful, or disappointed about not being able to join the trip, and your decision to go without her could exacerbate those feelings. As her partner, it's essential to prioritize empathy, understanding, and support during this challenging time. While it's true that you've supported her throughout the court process, this situation requires a different kind of support – emotional support and companionship. By choosing to stay with her or postpone the trip, you can demonstrate your commitment to your relationship and your willingness to prioritize her needs during a difficult time.
